voiceover: Two thousand years ago, a traveller reading Isaiah 53 asked the question everyone should ask. In Acts chapter 8, an Ethiopian official asks: about whom does the prophet say this — about himself, or about someone else? An ancient Jewish Aramaic translation, the Targum, names the servant in this song's first verse: my servant the Messiah. It redirects the servant's sufferings to Israel and the nations — but reading the Servant as the Messiah is not a Christian invention. The song itself gives clues. The servant is stricken for the transgression of my people — distinct from the people he suffers for. And he is innocent: he had done no violence, and there was no deceit in his mouth. And the song does not end at the grave. He poured out his soul to death — and after it, he shall see his offspring; he shall prolong his days. Innocent. Suffering for others. Dying — and then living on. And our oldest complete copy of Isaiah is dated to about 125 BC, long before Jesus. So who is it? Philip, beginning with this very Scripture, told him the good news about Jesus. Read Isaiah 53 for yourself.
